source: Lin et al. (2026) Know Before Fix: QA-Driven Repository Knowledge Acquisition for Software Issue Resolution (ACQUIRE)
finding: An agent that first asks and answers targeted questions about the repository (builds a model of the code) and only then edits beat a plain mini-SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified. The paper cites Vessey 1985 and Gugerty and Olson as the human basis. A single-pass 'proposal' (one root-cause plus fix hypothesis handed to the patcher) did worse than no pre-repair information at all.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3.2 + Mini-SWE-Agent baseline 66.4% Pass@1, ACQUIRE 70.8% (+4.4 pp), cost $0.055 -> $0.073 per instance. ACQUIRE-Proposal 66.0% (-4.8 pp vs ACQUIRE, below baseline). ACQUIRE-FreeQ (questions without category template) 67.0%. Net gain 22 resolved instances with 22 pass-to-fail regressions; 5 of 22 regressions had misleading QA framing, 17 were resolver-side. Rounds cut 7.1% overall, 17.1% on 44 FailPass instances. Steps 3,917 -> 3,246; locating -23.8%, fixing -24.1%. 232 audited QA pairs: 99.1% supported.
limits: Not token-matched: cost rose about 33%. Gain is +4.4 pp on one backbone; the GPT-5-mini column differs. About 70% of questions are 'mechanism' type. The Vessey link is cited in the discussion, not tested.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of gap 2: an explicit program-model step before the first edit helps a little, while one early hypothesis handed to the patcher hurts (hypothesis lock-in). Supports asking several narrow questions before editing and warns against a single committed cause.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid (VL/HCC)
finding: Controlled study of 20 developers debugging three small API bugs, with no aid, fault locations, or ready-made potential hypotheses. Having a correct hypothesis early predicted success. Giving fault locations did not help. Giving hypotheses helped a lot. Developers produced few hypotheses and most were wrong.
numbers: Control group: 2 hypotheses per defect; 27 hypotheses at stage 1, 11% correct (3); 25% (9) after stage 2; 39% (15) after stage 3. Correct hypothesis at stage 2 -> 5x more likely to fix (p=0.01). Potential hypotheses: odds ratio 6.24 (p=0.03), fault locations OR 1.4 (p=0.64), years of experience OR 1.14 (p=0.04). Fault-location group correct hypotheses 45% (stage 2) and 60% (stage 3) vs control 45% and 75%. Time to success not different (p=0.61).
limits: 25 recruited, 5 piloted, 60 sessions; small API bugs from Stack Overflow; hypotheses were simulated tool output with one correct and one wrong. Experience measured by years only.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that the quality of the early hypothesis (not where to look) is the lever. Gives a testable agent rule: log the first hypothesis and score it. Also warns that 'where' hints alone (fault localisation) may not help the patcher.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: Coded 30 hours of live-streamed professional work (15 sessions, 11 developers). Its Table 1 lists prior debugging-behaviour studies: Vessey 1985 is N=16, one organisation, about 6 hours; the larger strategy studies (Katz and Anderson N=77, Gugerty and Olson N=44) are mostly students.
numbers: 89 debugging episodes, over 15 h debugging and 13 h programming; 2,137 debugging activities and 1,407 programming activities; debugging once per 8 minutes of programming; no single activity dominated debugging time; most debug time sits in long episodes (some over 100 min).
limits: Observational, no expert/novice contrast, no test of breadth-first. Streamers self-select.
agent_relevance: Shows the empirical base for strategy claims is small and mostly lab or student. For gap 6: no larger-N professional replication of Vessey's classification appears in this table.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Qualitative theory from 7 professional developers plus 5 streamers on 17 debugging tasks. Debugging is described as updating a mental model of the system to guide information gathering, alternating navigation and execution, forward and backward tracing. Experience lets developers jump straight to likely places ('I know') and form hypotheses faster. Cites Vessey 1985.
numbers: 12 individuals, 17 tasks; 7 participants on 11 tasks totalling 7.8 hours. Participants had at least 3 years full-time experience.
limits: Only experienced developers were studied, so no expert versus novice contrast and no test of Vessey's counts. Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Independent modern support for the 'system model first, then targeted search' picture in professionals, but not a replication of Vessey's quantitative split. Closes part of gap 6 as conceptual agreement only.

source: Zhang, Roy and Arnaoudova (2025) Context-Specific Instruction: A Longitudinal Study on Debugging Skill Acquisition and Retention for Novice Programmers
finding: Eight-week study with 44 CS undergraduates (41 finished) on bug localisation. Teaching a concrete localisation procedure with problem-specific examples raised correctness far above no instruction, abstract guidelines, or concrete steps without context. Cites Vessey 1984 and 1985 for seeded faults and follow-ups.
numbers: Group 4 (context-specific): 80% correctness after one session and 80% after three weeks (CI 62-98%) vs 20-44% for the other groups, p<0.05 (Holm-adjusted). Time 13-15 min from session 1 vs 22-27 min. Baseline means G1 36% [8,65], G4 30% [2,58] (no baseline gap).
limits: Students, seeded logical faults in small programs, localisation only. Small groups (about 11 each). Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: A debugging strategy can be taught fast to novices, and generic abstract guidelines were weak. A scaffold should give worked, task-specific steps, not only rules like 'be breadth-first'.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) SWE-Explore: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Explore Repositories
finding: Benchmark of 848 issues, 10 languages, 203 repos that scores exploration alone with line-level ground truth taken from successful agent trajectories. Agentic explorers form a tier above classical retrieval. File-level hits are good, line-level recall is poor. Exploration metrics track downstream repair (Pearson up to 0.95 across explorers).
numbers: Restricted-context resolve rate (GPT-5.4 + Mini-SWE-Agent, K=5): Oracle 59.7, CoSIL 59.3, Codex 50.3, Mini-SWE-Agent 50.0, Claude Code 48.0, OpenHands 47.7, TF-IDF 26.0, RAG 23.3, BM25 12.7, Random 4.7. Correlation with resolve rate: context efficiency r=0.950, Rec@100 r=0.926 (Spearman 0.845), HitFile r=0.925. Agents HitFile about 0.64-0.68 but line recall 0.14-0.19; CoSIL recall 0.788, F1 0.602. Removing core evidence: resolve rate stays low until 50-75% of core regions are present; random extra code costs 7-9 pp only when no core evidence is present.
limits: Ground truth comes from trajectories of other agents (not a human-defined chunk). Correlations are across about 13 explorers, so n is small. Downstream patcher is fixed GPT-5.4 / Gemini-3-Pro.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 7: the useful unit is whatever puts the right evidence inside a small dense window (coverage plus compactness), and there is a threshold effect: partial evidence is nearly useless. Supports retrieving sets of co-needed regions rather than single best chunks. Function vs AST vs slice was not compared.

source: Al Awad and Ivanov (2026) Cost-Effective Repository Exploration for Agentic Issue Localization
finding: Treats repository exploration as a separate stage whose output is a ranked file list. Five explorer models on 499 SWE-bench Verified-derived tasks plus 500 tasks from 153 other repos. Cheaper models keep much of the quality at far less cost.
numbers: Lower-cost explorers keep about 78-94% of reference Hit@3 and 73-92% of F1, with agent time down 41-88% and tokens down 84-95%.
limits: Measures localisation only, not end-to-end repair; file-level units only; no flat versus hierarchical ablation.
agent_relevance: For gap 7, no clean evidence that hierarchy beats flat search; this paper only shows exploration is cheap to delegate. The hierarchy-vs-revisits question stays open.

source: Oderinwale (2026) Agent trajectories as programs: fingerprinting and programming coding-agent behavior (ProcGrep)
finding: Turns SWE-bench agent traces into compressed procedural vocabularies. Ten agents can be told apart from their habits. Behaviour is closest between models of similar release period or distilled from each other.
numbers: Probe attributes an unseen trajectory to the right agent at 85.7% (10 agents). Distilled student-teacher Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.25, about half the distance of other pairs.
limits: Describes habits, does not link them to solve rate; single author; no revisit or mode-switch counts in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Shows trace-level behaviour metrics are stable enough per model to measure, a prerequisite for Vessey-style counts (gap 1), but gives no outcome link.

source: Sahoo et al. (2026) AgentLens: Revealing The Lucky Pass Problem in SWE-Agent Evaluation
finding: Process-level scoring of 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from 8 backends on SWE-bench Verified. A composite process score separates passing from failing runs. Failing runs wander outside the known-good file space and loop more. Pass-rate and process-quality rankings disagree for all 8 models.
numbers: 1,136 passing trajectories: 229 Ideal (20.2%), 785 Solid (69.1%), 122 Lucky (10.7%). Composite score AUROC 0.766, accuracy 72.0%, F1 0.723, KS p=0.0017 (47 tasks, 1,815 trajectories); no single signal reached p<0.05. Failing runs 58% more likely to inspect files outside the known-good space (F/P 1.58); cyclic patterns 32% more prevalent (F/P 1.32). Lucky runs with blind retries waste 11.4 steps vs 2.7 in Ideal. Lucky rate 0.5% (Opus 4.5, pass 87.9%) to 23.2% (GPT-4.1, pass 59.9%).
limits: Reference paths are built from passing runs of the same tasks, so partly circular; not token-matched; only 47 of 60 tasks usable; AUROC 0.77 is moderate; one scaffold (OpenHands).
agent_relevance: Best available evidence for gap 1: process counts (out-of-space inspection, cycles, retries) predict outcome above chance, and wasteful loops cost steps. Not a Vessey metric and no revisit-cap intervention was tried.

source: Mehta and Datta (2026) When Agents Commit Too Soon: Diagnosing Premature Commitment in LLM Agents
finding: Measures how early hidden states of repeated ReAct runs settle (representational commitment). Settled runs vary less over the whole trajectory. The measure detects stability, not correctness. A prompt telling the agent to commit was tested.
numbers: Step-4 similarity vs whole-trajectory variability r=-0.35 (Llama-3.1-70B, HotpotQA); result vanishes on hard questions. Monitor from three partial runs: mean AUROC 0.81. Commitment prompt cut variability 28% vs a token-matched filler, not significant against the standard agent after correction, and no accuracy gain.
limits: Question answering (HotpotQA, StrategyQA), not code. Open-weight models with hidden-state access. Measures lock-in, not that lock-in lowers accuracy.
agent_relevance: Caution for gaps 1 and 2: early stability is easy to measure but is not the same as being wrong. A switch cap must be tested against accuracy, not variability.

source: Le et al. (2025) When Names Disappear: Revealing What LLMs Actually Understand About Code
finding: Strips or distorts identifier names while keeping behaviour. GPT-4o, Qwen3-Coder 480B, DeepSeek V3 and Llama 4 Maverick lose accuracy on summarising; execution prediction also drops. Misleading names cost a few points in most cells and no model gained. This is the 2025 large-model answer to gap 3: no expert-like gain under misleading names.
numbers: Summarisation class accuracy (ClassEval): GPT-4o 87.3 -> 58.7, DeepSeek V3 87.7 -> 76.7. Execution Pass@1 ClassEval original/misleading: GPT-4o 76.6/71.1, Qwen3-Coder 92.6/83.7, DeepSeek V3 90.0/88.8, Llama 4 81.1/80.8. LiveCodeBench: GPT-4o 82.9/82.3, Qwen3-Coder 99.3/93.8, DeepSeek V3 99.3/97.2, Llama 4 80.2/75.5. Ambiguous identifiers hurt more: DeepSeek V3 90.0 -> 69.3 (ClassEval), Llama 4 80.2 -> 56.4 (LiveCodeBench). Memorisation check: GPT-4o repeated the old output on 13 ClassEval samples originally, 2 under misleading names.
limits: No human expert group, so not the same task as Le et al. 2026; non-reasoning chat models from 2025; GPT-4o grades summaries; misleading names generated by an LLM; not 2026 frontier reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Names act as beacons for LLMs too, and misleading names hurt. On repos with poor names expect lower accuracy and add execution or test checks.

source: Abdelsalam et al. (2025) How do Humans and LLMs Process Confusing Code?
finding: Compares Qwen2.5-Coder-32B token perplexity with human EEG fixation-related potentials on Java snippets with 'atoms of confusion' (code that breaks reader expectations). Perplexity spikes where humans show confusion signals. A partial LLM analogue of the Soloway-Ehrlich cost of convention-breaking code (gap 4), but measured by perplexity, not recall.
numbers: Human data from Bergum et al.: 24 participants, 1,728 trials, 1,432 usable. Confusing snippets: Spearman rho=0.47, p<0.001 between max AOI perplexity and FRP amplitude; clean snippets rho=0.05, p=0.664. Perplexity difference confusing vs clean: effect size 0.42 (avg) and 0.45 (max), Wilcoxon p<0.001. Clean-atom overlap 0.38 [0.10, 0.70].
limits: Perplexity is not comprehension or recall; one 32B code model; short Java snippets; correlation only.
agent_relevance: LLM surprise lands where humans are surprised; a cheap way to flag convention-breaking regions for extra checking. Does not test scrambled-vs-coherent recall.

source: Machtle et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: Characterizing Code Comprehension Capabilities in (Large) Language Models
finding: On a CodeNet Python input-output consistency task, human-defined complexity metrics (size, control flow, AST) predict LLM success only weakly, while a feature-free shadow model predicts it much better. LLM difficulty is not human difficulty.
numbers: AUROC 0.63 for human-metric classifier (pruned 0.634 vs 0.554 for full-feature) vs 0.86 for shadow models. Two top open SWE-bench systems solved 234 and 230 tasks with 175 overlapping (59 and 55 unique).
limits: Binary I/O consistency is a narrow proxy for comprehension. Python only.
agent_relevance: Weakens the idea that human-style chunk complexity is the right difficulty measure for an LLM agent; use model-specific signals (retries, perplexity) instead.

source: Citation scan of Vessey (1985) and Vessey (1986) via Semantic Scholar and Crossref
finding: Scan of the first 300 papers that cite Vessey 1985 (Semantic Scholar list) found no title that re-runs her classification with a larger or second-language sample. Citers are mostly fault-localisation tools, education debugging reviews (Murphy 2008, Fitzgerald 2008, McCauley 2008) and comprehension models. Vessey's own 1986 follow-up analysed verbal-protocol content.
numbers: Vessey 1985 cited 295 times (Crossref), Vessey 1986 follow-up 82 times. Zero of 300 titles read as a replication.
limits: Title-level scan only; titles may hide replications. Texts of Murphy, Fitzgerald, Gugerty and Olson, Bednarik not opened (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: Vessey 1985 is a one-sample hypothesis. Use it for trace metrics, not as a rule.

source: Crossref metadata for founding recall and beacon studies: Shneiderman (1976); McKeithen et al. (1981); Wiedenbeck (1986); Soloway and Ehrlich (1984)
finding: Confirmed the primary papers exist and how often they are cited, but Crossref gives no abstracts and the full texts are paywalled. No effect sizes were obtained. Gap 9 stays open.
numbers: Citation counts: Shneiderman 1976 (Int J Comput Inf Sci) 150; Soloway and Ehrlich 1984 (IEEE TSE) 572; McKeithen et al. 1981 (Cognitive Psychology) 357; Wiedenbeck 1986 (Int J Man-Machine Studies) 45. DOIs 10.1007/bf00975629, 10.1109/tse.1984.5010283, 10.1016/0010-0285(81)90012-8, 10.1016/s0020-7373(86)80083-9.
limits: Metadata only; do not cite any numbers from these papers on this basis.
agent_relevance: None directly; keeps claim K07 at single-source/secondary.

source: Search log for gaps 3, 4, 8 and 10 (HuggingFace papers index queries, 2026-11-03)
finding: Queries for LLM scrambled-versus-coherent code recall, beacon studies on LLMs, template-style chunk storage for agents and human-graded replication of Glasz returned no matching study. Closest hits were the obfuscation study (d11) and the perplexity-versus-EEG study (d12). Gaps 4, 8 and 10 remain open as 'not found', not as 'shown absent'.
numbers: About 20 queries over several index calls; 0 direct matches. WebSearch budget was exhausted by other agents, the arXiv API returned empty bodies, OpenAlex was rate-limited.
limits: Absence of evidence under a rate-limited search is weak; a later pass should retry arXiv and Semantic Scholar.
agent_relevance: Treat gap 4 as an experiment to run, not a fact to cite: shuffle statement order, ask a model to reproduce the code, compare with coherent versions across model sizes.
